$comment: The substrate below the game. NEVER craftable, never on the shelf — it only appears at the bottom of a provenance tree, so the chain ends in real chemistry instead of stopping at a rock. Composition, not provenance: the craft tree says where a thing came from, this says what it is made of.

atoms.name: Hydrogen
atoms.fact: The first element, made in the first minutes of the universe. Everything else came later.

atoms.name: Helium
atoms.fact: The ash of the Sun. Four hydrogen nuclei, fused, with a little mass left over as light.

atoms.name: Lithium
atoms.fact: Light enough to float on water — one of only three metals that can.

atoms.name: Beryllium
atoms.fact: Pulled out of emerald and beryl in 1798, when a chemist dissolved the crystals in alkali and found an unknown 'earth' left behind.

atoms.name: Boron
atoms.fact: Isolated in 1808 by running electric current through a borate solution and scraping the brown residue off the electrode.

atoms.name: Carbon
atoms.fact: Four bonds, in every direction, endlessly. Every molecule life is built from hangs off carbon.

atoms.name: Nitrogen
atoms.fact: Four fifths of the air, and almost impossible for life to reach until something fixes it.

atoms.name: Oxygen
atoms.fact: Most of your body's mass. Forged inside stars and scattered when they died.

atoms.name: Fluorine
atoms.fact: Took 74 years of failed, sometimes dangerous, attempts before Henri Moissan finally isolated it in 1886.

atoms.name: Neon
atoms.fact: When it was first coaxed into glowing in 1898, the discoverer called the crimson light "a sight to dwell upon and never forget."

atoms.name: Sodium
atoms.fact: Half of salt, and the reason a nerve can fire.

atoms.name: Magnesium
atoms.fact: One atom sits at the centre of every chlorophyll molecule. Green is magnesium.

atoms.name: Aluminium
atoms.fact: The commonest metal in the crust, and locked so tightly into rock it was a precious metal until 1886.

atoms.name: Silicon
atoms.fact: After oxygen, the commonest element in the crust. Every rock, every grain of sand.

atoms.name: Phosphorus
atoms.fact: Carries the energy and holds the DNA backbone together. The scarcest of the six.

atoms.name: Sulfur
atoms.fact: Two amino acids carry it. It is also why onion and garlic fight back.

atoms.name: Chlorine
atoms.fact: The other half of salt. Lethal as a gas, essential as an ion.

atoms.name: Argon
atoms.fact: Found in 1894 by stripping every known gas out of air and noticing something was still left over.

atoms.name: Potassium
atoms.fact: Leached out of ash as potash. Plants cannot grow without it.

atoms.name: Calcium
atoms.fact: Shell, bone, chalk and limestone are all the same idea.

atoms.name: Scandium
atoms.fact: Predicted by Mendeleev in 1869 as 'eka-boron,' a full ten years before anyone actually found it.

atoms.name: Titanium
atoms.fact: Discovered because black sand in a Cornish stream stuck to a magnet — the mineral turned out to hide a new metal.

atoms.name: Vanadium
atoms.fact: Discovered once in 1801, then talked out of it by a French chemist who insisted it was just chromium — it took thirty years and a second discovery to stick.

atoms.name: Chromium
atoms.fact: Isolated in 1797 by heating its oxide in a charcoal oven until metal came out the other side.

atoms.name: Manganese
atoms.fact: Ground into pigment for cave paintings at Lascaux and Gargas — some of that art is over 30,000 years old, and the color is manganese.

atoms.name: Iron
atoms.fact: The last thing a dying star can make without exploding.

atoms.name: Cobalt
atoms.fact: A radioactive form of it, cobalt-60, was used in a famous 1950s experiment that proved nature doesn't always play fair — it violates a symmetry called parity.

atoms.name: Nickel
atoms.fact: Discovered in 1751 by a chemist trying to extract copper from an ore that stubbornly refused — he named the impostor metal after a mischievous mining spirit.

atoms.name: Copper
atoms.fact: One of only a handful of metals that isn't gray or silver — its orange-red color comes from a quirk in how it absorbs light.

atoms.name: Zinc
atoms.fact: Alchemists called its oxide 'philosopher's wool,' because burning zinc metal left woolly white tufts behind.

atoms.name: Gallium
atoms.fact: Melts at 29.76°C — just above room temperature, so a solid piece will turn liquid sitting in your palm.

atoms.name: Germanium
atoms.fact: Predicted by Mendeleev seventeen years before anyone found it — he called it 'eka-silicon' and got its properties eerily close to right.

atoms.name: Arsenic
atoms.fact: Victorian women ate it, mixed with vinegar and chalk, to whiten their skin — proof of a life that didn't require working outdoors.

atoms.name: Selenium
atoms.fact: Found in 1817 because a red residue smelled like horseradish when burned — a smell close enough to tellurium's that it took a careful chemist to tell them apart.

atoms.name: Bromine
atoms.fact: One of only two elements that's a liquid at room temperature — the other is mercury.

atoms.name: Krypton
atoms.fact: Defined the length of a meter for 23 years — from 1960 to 1983, the meter was officially a count of krypton-86 light waves.

atoms.name: Rubidium
atoms.fact: Found by its fingerprint in a flame: the second element ever discovered by spectroscope, a year after the instrument existed.

atoms.name: Strontium
atoms.fact: Named for the Scottish village of Strontian, where the ore didn't behave like the other 'heavy spars' it was mistaken for.

atoms.name: Yttrium
atoms.fact: In 1987, a compound of yttrium, barium, and copper became only the second material ever found to superconduct above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen — the discovery that made superconductors cheap to cool.

atoms.name: Zirconium
atoms.fact: Its powder burns in bright white sparks, which is why it turns up in fireworks and flashbulbs.

atoms.name: Niobium
atoms.fact: Alloyed with tin, it keeps superconducting even under strong magnetic fields — the 1961 discovery that made powerful electromagnets for MRI machines and particle accelerators possible.

atoms.name: Molybdenum
atoms.fact: British tanks in WWI swapped their heavy manganese-steel armor for molybdenum steel — lighter, faster, and just as tough.

atoms.name: Technetium
atoms.fact: A radioactive form of it, technetium-99m, is injected into roughly ten million people a year for medical imaging — the workhorse isotope of nuclear medicine.

atoms.name: Ruthenium
atoms.fact: Found in 1844 in the leftover sludge from minting Russian rubles out of platinum — named for Russia.

atoms.name: Rhodium
atoms.fact: Named for the Greek word for rose, after the rose-red salt its discoverer extracted from dissolved platinum ore in 1803.

atoms.name: Palladium
atoms.fact: Named after the asteroid Pallas — which had been discovered only two months before, and which people still thought was a planet at the time.

atoms.name: Silver
atoms.fact: During WWII the US wound 13,540 tons of it into electromagnets for enriching uranium — copper was too scarce to spare for the job.

atoms.name: Cadmium
atoms.fact: Discovered in 1817 as a hidden impurity in pharmacy shelf zinc — a batch that changed color on heating gave it away.

atoms.name: Indium
atoms.fact: Soft enough to dent with a fingernail, cut with a butter knife, or bite into — and it leaves a gray streak on paper like a soft pencil.

atoms.name: Tin
atoms.fact: Bend a bar of it and it crackles — the 'tin cry,' caused by crystals inside twisting past each other.

atoms.name: Antimony
atoms.fact: Grind it the wrong way in a mortar and pestle and it can detonate — an unnerving trait for something that looks like an ordinary gray solid.

atoms.name: Tellurium
atoms.fact: Australian miners once used a gold-bearing ore of it to fill potholes, not realizing what it was — when they figured it out in 1896, they dug up the streets.

atoms.name: Iodine
atoms.fact: Usually a dull violet, but drop it in fuming sulfuric acid and it turns a startling bright blue.

atoms.name: Xenon
atoms.fact: In 1989 IBM scientists spelled out their company's name using 35 individual xenon atoms — the first time anyone had arranged atoms on purpose.

atoms.name: Caesium
atoms.fact: Melts in a warm room, at 28.5°C. Soft enough to dent with a fingernail — the softest metal there is.

atoms.name: Barium
atoms.fact: Burns with a green flame bright enough to be a reliable test for its presence.

atoms.name: Lanthanum
atoms.fact: Named for the Greek 'to lie hidden' — it hid inside cerium ore, masked by nearly identical chemistry, for years.

atoms.name: Cerium
atoms.fact: The first rare earth found, and still the easiest to pull out — the only lanthanide that holds a stable +4 charge in water.

atoms.name: Praseodymium
atoms.fact: Tarnishes green in air, flaking apart the way iron rusts — a fist-sized piece corrodes completely within a year.

atoms.name: Neodymium
atoms.fact: A neodymium magnet a few grams heavy can lift a thousand times its own weight — and snap together hard enough to break a finger.

atoms.name: Promethium
atoms.fact: Named for Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods — fitting for an element that's a marvel and faintly dangerous to hold.

atoms.name: Samarium
atoms.fact: The first element ever named after a real person — a Russian mine official named Vasili Samarsky, who had no say in it.

atoms.name: Europium
atoms.fact: So reactive that a fist-sized chunk oxidizes completely within days — the shine barely lasts long enough to see.

atoms.name: Gadolinium
atoms.fact: One isotope of it, gadolinium-157, soaks up neutrons better than any other stable atom known — 259,000 barns worth.

atoms.name: Terbium
atoms.fact: One of four elements named after the same tiny Swedish village, Ytterby — a mining quarry that also gave its name to yttrium, erbium, and ytterbium.

atoms.name: Dysprosium
atoms.fact: Took its discoverer more than thirty attempts to isolate — he named it from the Greek for 'hard to get.'

atoms.name: Holmium
atoms.fact: Has the strongest magnetic pull of any element found in nature, and gets packed into magnets to generate the most powerful fields humans can make.

atoms.name: Erbium
atoms.fact: Its ions amplify light at exactly the wavelength optical fiber loses least — which is why erbium is part of what makes transoceanic internet cables work.

atoms.name: Thulium
atoms.fact: Glows blue under ultraviolet light, which is why a trace of it is baked into euro banknotes as an anti-forgery mark.

atoms.name: Ytterbium
atoms.fact: Has the narrowest liquid range of any metal — melts at 824°C and boils again just 372 degrees later.

atoms.name: Lutetium
atoms.fact: A radioactive form of it, bound to a hormone-mimicking molecule, is used to hunt down and irradiate neuroendocrine tumors from the inside.

atoms.name: Hafnium
atoms.fact: Its carbide is the most heat-resistant compound known — it doesn't melt until almost 3,900°C.

atoms.name: Tantalum
atoms.fact: Named for Tantalus, the mythical figure eternally denied food and water — this metal is so inert it can sit in acid and refuse to be dissolved.

atoms.name: Tungsten
atoms.fact: Has the highest melting point of any element — 3,422°C, hot enough that almost nothing else is still solid.

atoms.name: Rhenium
atoms.fact: A Japanese chemist found it in 1908 and thought it was a different, lighter element entirely — the mistake wasn't corrected by X-ray analysis until just before his death, twenty-two years later.

atoms.name: Osmium
atoms.fact: The densest element that doesn't decay — about twice as dense as lead.

atoms.name: Iridium
atoms.fact: Named for Iris, the rainbow goddess, because the salts its discoverer made from it came in a startling range of colors.

atoms.name: Platinum
atoms.fact: Pre-Columbian metalworkers in South America figured out how to shape it centuries before Europeans could — by sintering it with gold powder into a workable alloy.

atoms.name: Gold
atoms.fact: A single gram can be hammered into a sheet a full square meter wide, or drawn into a wire one atom thick before it finally snaps.

atoms.name: Mercury
atoms.fact: The first element ever caught superconducting — cooled below 4 Kelvin in 1911, right after liquid helium first became available to chill things that cold.

atoms.name: Thallium
atoms.fact: Announced itself as a bright green line in a spectroscope in 1861 — its name comes from the Greek word for a green shoot.

atoms.name: Lead
atoms.fact: Turns superconducting below 7.19 Kelvin — the highest transition temperature of any simple, type-I superconductor.

atoms.name: Bismuth
atoms.fact: Expands as it solidifies instead of shrinking, which made it useful in printing-press alloys where it offset the metals that did shrink.

atoms.name: Polonium
atoms.fact: By weight, about 250,000 times more toxic than cyanide — a gram of polonium-210 could in principle poison twenty million people.

atoms.name: Astatine
atoms.fact: So radioactive that a visible piece would instantly vaporize itself — no one has ever seen a lump of it.

atoms.name: Radon
atoms.fact: Discovered in 1899 as a gas continually seeping out of radium — the fifth radioactive element ever found, and the only one of the first five that's a gas.

atoms.name: Francium
atoms.fact: So radioactive it has never been seen in bulk — any visible amount would boil itself away from its own decay heat.

atoms.name: Radium
atoms.fact: The Curies found it by process of elimination: pull all the uranium out of pitchblende, and the ore was still radioactive. Something else was in there.

atoms.name: Actinium
atoms.fact: Glows pale blue in the dark — its own radioactivity ionizing the air around it.

atoms.name: Thorium
atoms.fact: Once lit the world: heated in a gas mantle, its oxide burns an intense white.

atoms.name: Protactinium
atoms.fact: In 1961 the UK spent half a million dollars processing sixty tonnes of waste to recover 127 grams of it — the world's only significant supply for decades.

atoms.name: Uranium
atoms.fact: Named for a planet, not a person. Klaproth spotted it in pitchblende in 1789 and thought of Uranus, discovered only eight years before.

atoms.name: Neptunium
atoms.fact: Made by bombarding uranium with neutrons in 1940. Named for the next planet out — the same logic that named uranium itself.

atoms.name: Plutonium
atoms.fact: Left in damp air it swells by seventy percent, flaking into a powder that catches fire on its own.

atoms.name: Americium
atoms.fact: Its discovery was a Manhattan Project secret — until Glenn Seaborg let it slip on a children's radio quiz show, five days before the official announcement.

atoms.name: Curium
atoms.fact: Radioactive enough to glow purple in the dark, lit by its own alpha particles ionizing the air.

atoms.name: Berkelium
atoms.fact: Named for Berkeley, the city where it was made — following the same habit that named terbium after a Swedish village.

atoms.name: Californium
atoms.fact: One microgram of californium-252 throws off 2.3 million neutrons a second — a speck that's genuinely dangerous to be near.

atoms.name: Einsteinium
atoms.fact: First found in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb test, in 1952 — the only element discovered inside a mushroom cloud.

atoms.name: Fermium
atoms.fact: Pulled from the debris of that same 1952 hydrogen bomb test. Two elements, one explosion.

atoms.name: Mendelevium
atoms.fact: The first element ever made one atom at a time — seventeen atoms, total, in the whole 1955 discovery.

atoms.name: Nobelium
atoms.fact: Breaks the actinide pattern: in solution it prefers to lose two electrons, not three, behaving more like calcium than its neighbors.

atoms.name: Lawrencium
atoms.fact: Its outermost electron sits in a p-orbital instead of the d-orbital every other actinide uses — a one-element exception to the pattern.

atoms.name: Rutherfordium
atoms.fact: Its name took over three decades to settle — American and Soviet teams both claimed the discovery, and the dispute wasn't resolved until 1997.

atoms.name: Dubnium
atoms.fact: Its longest-lived known form lasts about 16 hours before decaying — barely enough time to run an experiment on it.

atoms.name: Seaborgium
atoms.fact: Named after Glenn Seaborg while he was still alive to see it — one of only two elements ever given that honor.

atoms.name: Bohrium
atoms.fact: Confirmed from just five atoms, made in 1981 by firing chromium nuclei at a bismuth target.

atoms.name: Hassium
atoms.fact: Named for Hesse, the German state where the lab that made it sits — from the old Latin name for the region, Hassia.

atoms.name: Meitnerium
atoms.fact: The only element named specifically for a real, non-mythological woman — physicist Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission and was denied the Nobel Prize for it.

atoms.name: Darmstadtium
atoms.fact: Its most stable known form lasts about 14 seconds — long by superheavy-element standards, and still barely enough to notice.

atoms.name: Roentgenium
atoms.fact: Named for Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays — one of the few elements named for a discovery rather than a place.

atoms.name: Copernicium
atoms.fact: Named on Nicolaus Copernicus's birthday — specifically the 537th anniversary of it, in 2010.

atoms.name: Nihonium
atoms.fact: Named for Japan — the country's second attempt at claiming an element, after an earlier 'nipponium' claim was rejected decades before.

atoms.name: Flerovium
atoms.fact: Confirmed by a single atom, in 1998, that stuck around for about 30 seconds before decaying — that one atom was the whole discovery.

atoms.name: Moscovium
atoms.fact: First made in 2003 — four atoms total, each gone within about a tenth of a second.

atoms.name: Livermorium
atoms.fact: Its first 'discovery,' claimed in 1999, turned out to be fabricated data from one scientist — the real element wasn't confirmed until years later, with actual atoms.

atoms.name: Tennessine
atoms.fact: The berkelium needed to make it crossed the Atlantic five times — Russian customs kept turning back the shipment — and had to arrive before the target decayed past use.

atoms.name: Oganesson
atoms.fact: Should, by the usual noble-gas logic, be a gas — but relativistic effects are expected to make it a solid at room temperature instead.

compounds.name: Water
compounds.fact: Two hydrogens at an angle, which is why water is sticky, why ice floats, and why life works.

compounds.name: Silica
compounds.fact: Quartz. It survives weathering better than almost anything, which is why sand is mostly this.

compounds.name: Feldspar
compounds.fact: Around half of granite, and the mineral that weathers down into clay.

compounds.name: Mica
compounds.fact: Splits into sheets thin enough to see through. The dark flecks in granite.

compounds.name: Calcium Carbonate
compounds.fact: Chalk, limestone, eggshell and seashell. Life's favourite building material.

compounds.name: Rock Salt
compounds.fact: A cube of alternating ions. The only mineral humans eat by the spoonful.

compounds.name: Glucose
compounds.fact: What photosynthesis actually makes. Every other food molecule is built from it or burnt into it.

compounds.name: Starch
compounds.fact: Thousands of glucose units chained up for storage. A seed's packed lunch.

compounds.name: Cellulose
compounds.fact: The same glucose, bonded the other way round — and that one flip is why we can eat bread but not wood.

compounds.name: Amino Acid
compounds.fact: Twenty of them, in every living thing on Earth, all the same handedness. No exception has ever been found.

compounds.name: Protein
compounds.fact: A chain folded into one specific shape. The shape is the function — and it is decided entirely by the order of the links.
compounds.note: Built from the twenty amino acids. Each bond formed releases one water molecule, which is why a residue in a chain is lighter than the free acid it came from.

compounds.name: Fatty Acid
compounds.fact: A long carbon tail that will not mix with water. That refusal is what makes a cell membrane possible.

compounds.name: Fat
compounds.fact: Twice the energy per gram of sugar, which is why seeds and animals both store it.

compounds.name: Nucleotide
compounds.fact: Sugar, phosphate and a base. Four of them spell out everything alive.

compounds.name: DNA
compounds.fact: The instructions for building the thing you are holding, written in four letters.

compounds.name: Chlorophyll
compounds.fact: Catches the photon and hands its energy to chemistry. One magnesium atom sits at the centre.

compounds.name: Sunlight
compounds.fact: Eight minutes and nineteen seconds old when it reaches the leaf. Not matter at all — the only thing here that is pure energy.

compounds.name: Hydrogen Fusion
compounds.fact: Four hydrogen nuclei become one helium, and the missing mass leaves as light. That light is the entire energy budget of this game.

compounds.name: Glycerol
compounds.fact: A three-carbon spine with three hooks. Hang a fatty acid on each and you have a fat.

compounds.name: Polypeptide Chain
compounds.fact: Amino acids in a line, in a specific order. The order is written in DNA and read by a ribosome.

compounds.name: Helix & Sheet
compounds.fact: The chain coils into helices and pleats into sheets, held only by hydrogen bonds along the backbone.

compounds.name: Fold
compounds.fact: Helices and sheets pack into one compact shape, usually within a second of being made.

compounds.name: Enzyme
compounds.fact: A protein with a pocket shaped to hold one particular molecule. Nearly every step in this game is one of these doing its job.

compounds.name: Membrane
compounds.fact: Two layers of fat, tails inward, because the tails will not tolerate water. Life needs an inside, and this is how it gets one.

compounds.name: Cell
compounds.fact: The smallest thing that is unambiguously alive. Everything you have eaten was made of these.

compounds.name: Muscle
compounds.fact: Cells packed with protein filaments that ratchet past each other. Meat is this, rested.

compounds.name: Epithelium
compounds.fact: Cells packed edge to edge with almost no space between them, stitched together by their own cadherins and keratin. Skin's outer face is this.

compounds.name: Connective Tissue
compounds.fact: Cells scattered through fiber and fluid instead of packed together. Collagen fiber is a quarter of all the protein in a mammal, and this is where most of it lives.

compounds.name: Nervous Tissue
compounds.fact: Neurons that fire, and glial cells that keep them fed and insulated in a fatty myelin sheath.

compounds.name: Heart
compounds.fact: Cardiac muscle does the squeezing, a collagen framework gives the wall its shape, epithelium lines every chamber, and its own pacemaker cells set the beat.

compounds.name: Lung
compounds.fact: Epithelium lines the airway down to the alveoli, elastic and collagen fiber let the tissue recoil, smooth muscle rings the bronchioles, and the vagus nerve reaches in to set their width.

compounds.name: Brain
compounds.fact: Composed primarily of two kinds of cell: neurons that signal, and the glial cells that support, feed and insulate them.

compounds.name: Liver
compounds.fact: Epithelium lines its bile ducts, and a fibrous connective-tissue capsule wraps the whole organ and threads through it, carrying the vessels in.

compounds.name: Skin
compounds.fact: Epithelium on the outside, connective tissue beneath it cushioning every stress, nerve endings that sense touch, and a tiny muscle at the root of every hair.

compounds.name: Kidney
compounds.fact: At least 26 distinct cell types, epithelial, endothelial, stromal and smooth muscle among them, all wrapped in a tough fibrous capsule and wired to the renal plexus.

compounds.name: Elephant Heart
compounds.fact: Its apex splits into two points instead of one — an unusual trait among mammals, shared only with the sirenians, manatees and dugongs.

compounds.name: Elephant Lung
compounds.fact: No pleural cavity — connective tissue fills that space instead, fusing lung straight to diaphragm, which may be what lets an elephant equalize pressure while it snorkels on its trunk.

compounds.name: Elephant Brain
compounds.fact: The largest brain of any terrestrial mammal — 4.5 to 5.5 kilograms, its temporal lobes so oversized they bulge out to the sides of the skull.

compounds.name: Elephant Skin
compounds.fact: An inch thick over the back and head — tough enough to look armored, yet sensitive enough to need a daily mud bath against burning and insect bites.

compounds.name: Chicken Lung
compounds.fact: No in-and-out breath: air sacs push air one way through the lung, their walls nothing but epithelium laid over an elastic connective-tissue scaffold, barely touched by a blood vessel.

compounds.name: Chicken Heart
compounds.fact: Four chambers, like a mammal's — a design birds evolved on their own, shared only with the crocodilians among reptiles, built to move enough oxygen for constant high activity.

compounds.name: Chicken Kidney
compounds.fact: No urinary bladder — nearly no bird has one. Urine runs straight from ureter to cloaca, the one opening that serves as reservoir for urine, dung and egg alike.

compounds.name: Chicken Brain
compounds.fact: No layered cortex — neurons cluster into three-dimensional nuclei instead, in a pallium that does a mammal cortex's job well enough to give birds a large brain-to-body ratio and real intelligence.

compounds.name: Bone Tissue
compounds.fact: About 30% flexible collagen matrix and 70% bound calcium phosphate mineral, laid down by osteoblasts and steadily broken back down by osteoclasts — never finished, always being rebuilt.

compounds.name: Cartilage
compounds.fact: Chondrocytes packed in their own matrix of collagen and proteoglycan, with no blood vessels reaching in at all — cut off from blood, and free of feeling because of it.

compounds.name: Ligament
compounds.fact: Bone tied straight to bone: dense bundles of collagen fiber, with no muscle involved at all — that job belongs to a tendon instead.

compounds.name: Patella
compounds.fact: The largest sesamoid bone in the human body — grown inside the quadriceps tendon itself rather than jointed to a neighbour, which lets it increase the leverage that tendon can put through the knee.

compounds.name: Tibia
compounds.fact: The shin bone — second largest bone in the body after the femur, and the one whose upper surface actually meets the femur to carry weight through the knee.

compounds.name: Skull
compounds.fact: Forty-four separate bony pieces at birth, fused through the closing fontanelles down to twenty-two by adulthood — eight cranial, fourteen facial — built to keep the brain from injury.

compounds.name: Mandible
compounds.fact: The skull's only movable bone — every other piece is fixed in place, while the jaw alone hinges at both temples, and still counts as the strongest bone in the face.

compounds.name: Spine
compounds.fact: A segmented stack of vertebrae running the length of the back, wrapped around the spinal cord the whole way down to protect it.

compounds.name: Rib Cage
compounds.fact: Twelve pairs of ribs closed by the sternum in front and anchored to the thoracic vertebrae in back — a cage built around the heart and lungs, not just near them.

compounds.name: Pelvis
compounds.fact: A pair of hip bones fused to the sacrum and coccyx behind them, forming the bowl that carries the whole upper body's weight down into the legs.

compounds.name: Femur
compounds.fact: The longest and thickest bone in the human body — strong enough that some measures call it the strongest bone there is, though the temporal bone gives it real competition.

compounds.name: Synovial Fluid
compounds.fact: Blood plasma filtered thin and thickened with hyaluronan and lubricin, so a joint's surfaces can slide against each other without ever actually touching.

compounds.name: Knee
compounds.fact: Really two joints in one: femur meets tibia to carry weight, femur meets patella to lever the quadriceps — the whole thing held by ligament, cushioned by cartilage, and bathed in synovial fluid throughout.

compounds.name: Skeleton
compounds.fact: Around 270 bones at birth, fused down to about 206 by adulthood — the frame that holds the body's shape, shields the organs inside it, and gives every joint something to move against.

compounds.name: Hematopoietic Stem Cell
compounds.fact: A small, self-renewing population in the marrow that gives rise to every other blood cell — splitting into a myeloid line and a lymphoid line, which between them build every red cell, white cell and platelet in circulation.

compounds.name: Neutrophil
compounds.fact: 40 to 70 percent of all white blood cells, more than any other kind — a short-lived cell with a nucleus split into two to five lobes, usually the first one to reach a site of infection.

compounds.name: Lymphocyte
compounds.fact: T cells and B cells run the adaptive immune response between them — B cells manufacture antibodies against a pathogen, and cytotoxic T cells kill the cells it has already infected.

compounds.name: Monocyte
compounds.fact: The largest white blood cell in circulation, and only briefly — after one to three days in the bloodstream it moves into body tissue and becomes a macrophage or dendritic cell, the phagocyte that does the actual eating.

compounds.name: Megakaryocyte
compounds.fact: A bone marrow cell ten to fifteen times the size of a red blood cell, its nucleus copied over past the ordinary two sets of DNA — grown that large for one purpose, to break its own cytoplasm into thousands of platelets.

compounds.name: Hemoglobin
compounds.fact: Four folded protein chains, each cradling an iron-holding heme group — the iron is what actually grabs an oxygen molecule and lets blood carry it from the lungs to every other tissue.

compounds.name: Red Blood Cell
compounds.fact: Built with no nucleus and no organelles at all — both are expelled during development to clear more room for hemoglobin, which ends up filling about a third of the cell's total volume.

compounds.name: Platelet
compounds.fact: Not actually a cell — just a fragment of cytoplasm broken off a megakaryocyte, with no nucleus of its own, that clumps at the site of an injured vessel to start a clot.

compounds.name: Plasma
compounds.fact: Up to 95 percent water, carrying the dissolved albumin, globulins and fibrinogen that hold osmotic pressure steady, fight infection and clot a wound — every blood cell rides suspended in it, not part of it.

compounds.name: Bone Marrow
compounds.fact: Red marrow is where the body actually builds its blood, turning out about 500 billion new blood cells a day from hematopoietic stem cells held in a reticular connective-tissue framework — the yellow marrow further out in the skeleton has converted almost entirely to fat and does none of it.

compounds.name: Blood
compounds.fact: Blood cells suspended in plasma — by volume roughly 45 percent red cells and 54 percent plasma, with white cells making up less than one percent, though white cells and platelets do nearly all of the immune and clotting work.

compounds.name: Chicken Crop
compounds.fact: A thin-walled pouch off the esophagus where swallowed feed waits before digestion even starts — chickens keep one, along with turkeys, ducks, geese and parrots.

compounds.name: Proventriculus
compounds.fact: The bird's glandular 'true stomach' — secretory glands lining it add hydrochloric acid and pepsinogen to the feed, and it contracts on its own to help mix everything before the gizzard takes over.

compounds.name: Gizzard
compounds.fact: Muscular bands grind food the way teeth would in a bird that has none, protected from their own crushing by a multi-layered koilin lining laid down over the muscle.

compounds.name: Small Intestine
compounds.fact: Villi comb the epithelial lining for absorption, two layers of smooth muscle drive peristalsis, and its own nerve plexuses — Meissner's in the submucosa, Auerbach's between the muscle layers — run largely independent of the brain.

compounds.name: Ceca
compounds.fact: Blind pouches at the junction of the small and large intestine, usually paired in a bird — though not always: parrots have none at all, and the secretarybird carries two full pairs.

compounds.name: Large Intestine
compounds.fact: Water and salts are pulled back out through a lining of simple columnar epithelium that dips down into intestinal glands, while muscle keeps everything moving along toward the cloaca.

compounds.name: Cloaca
compounds.fact: One rear opening does the job of three systems — in birds, as in amphibians, reptiles and cartilaginous fish, the digestive, reproductive and urinary tracts all exit through this single vent.

compounds.name: Esophagus
compounds.fact: Muscle switches type on the way down — striated at the top for a voluntary swallow, smooth at the bottom for the involuntary squeeze that finishes it — with the myenteric plexus threaded between the layers.

compounds.name: Stomach
compounds.fact: Glandular epithelium supplies gastric juice's acid and pepsinogen, three muscle layers churn it — including an oblique layer found nowhere else in the gut — inside a connective-tissue serosa laced with the myenteric plexus.

compounds.name: Gallbladder
compounds.fact: Concentrates the liver's bile three- to tenfold, pulling out water and salts behind a microvilli-brushed epithelial lining and a smooth-muscle layer running longitudinal, oblique and transverse all at once.

compounds.name: Pancreas
compounds.fact: Ninety-nine percent exocrine, one percent endocrine: acinar cells in thin fibrous-walled lobes push out digestive enzymes, while scattered islets of Langerhans answer for the insulin instead.

compounds.name: Small Intestine
compounds.fact: Duodenum, jejunum and ileum in series — villi comb the epithelial lining for absorption, two muscle layers drive peristalsis, and Meissner's and Auerbach's plexuses run it largely independent of the brain.

compounds.name: Large Intestine
compounds.fact: Taeniae coli — muscle ribbons shorter than the tube itself — gather it into pouch-like haustra, while glands sunk into the epithelium pull water and salts back out for over 700 resident bacterial species to finish.

compounds.name: Appendix
compounds.fact: Reassessed since the early 2000s, no longer written off as vestigial: gut-associated lymphoid tissue packs its wall, standing immune watch and, per one 2007 hypothesis, sheltering the gut's bacteria through illness or antibiotics.

compounds.name: Anal Canal
compounds.fact: Two sphincters, not one: an inner ring under involuntary control, an outer ring the body can clench at will, wrapped around a lining that changes type on the way out — columnar, then squamous, keratinized at the skin.

compounds.name: N-Acetylglucosamine
compounds.fact: An amide derivative of glucose — swap one hydroxyl for an acetamide group, and this is the monomer chitin is built from.

compounds.name: Chitin
compounds.fact: A long chain of N-acetylglucosamine units — the same structural molecule that stiffens a mushroom's cell wall and a crab's shell, here built into every insect's exoskeleton.

compounds.name: Insect Cuticle
compounds.fact: Not skin, not bone — fibrous chitin set in a protein matrix, laid down in layers by a sheet of living epidermal cells underneath it. Every tube, plate and joint an insect has is built from this.

compounds.name: Spiracle
compounds.fact: An opening in the exoskeleton itself, not a separate structure — its own ring of closer muscle opens it to admit air and shuts it again to hold water in.

compounds.name: Trachea
compounds.fact: Reinforced from inside by taenidia — a thin, spiral 'wire' of its own cuticle winding through the wall so the tube can flex and stretch like a vacuum hose without collapsing.

compounds.name: Tracheole
compounds.fact: Where the tube finally ends: a single cell wraps each fine branch, keeping its tip filled with fluid so oxygen can dissolve and cross straight into the cytoplasm of the cell next door.

compounds.name: Tracheal System
compounds.fact: Air runs spiracle to trachea to tracheole to cell, with no lung and no heartbeat in the chain — the blood does not carry oxygen at all, only nutrients, circulating loose in an open hemocoel instead of vessels.

compounds.name: Malpighian Tubules
compounds.fact: Fine tubes closed at one end, a single layer of cells thick, floating loose in the hemolymph. Ions get pumped into the tube and water follows by osmosis, until what's left precipitates into uric acid once it reaches the hindgut.

compounds.name: Ecdysone
compounds.fact: The prohormone of 20-hydroxyecdysone, the insect molting hormone proper — secreted from the prothoracic glands, and a rise in its concentration is what switches on the genes a larva needs for its next molt.

compounds.name: Juvenile Hormone
compounds.fact: Secreted by the corpora allata, a pair of glands behind the brain — in a honey bee, plenty of it keeps ecdysone driving larva-to-larva molts, less of it switches ecdysone over to pupation, and its complete absence is what finally lets the adult form.

compounds.name: Foregut
compounds.fact: An invagination of the epidermis, lined with cuticle just like the exoskeleton outside it — this is the section that stores, grinds and moves food onward, and the whole lining sheds with every moult, right along with the rest of the exoskeleton.

compounds.name: Midgut
compounds.fact: Unlike the gut sections on either side of it, this one isn't lined with cuticle at all — just rapidly dividing epithelial cells, constantly replacing themselves while secreting the enzymes that digest the food and absorb the nutrients.

compounds.name: Hindgut
compounds.fact: Cuticle-lined like the foregut, and shed with it at every moult — three sections, the ileum, the colon and the wide rectum, doing the last work of reclaiming water and salt before what's left becomes a fecal pellet.

compounds.name: Hemolymph
compounds.fact: Water carrying dissolved salts, sugar and protein, plus free-floating hemocyte cells for immune defense — and unlike vertebrate blood, none of it carries oxygen: that job belongs entirely to the tracheal system instead.

compounds.name: Dorsal Vessel
compounds.fact: A muscular tube running the length of the body, not a chambered pump — hemolymph seeps in through many small one-way channels along its length, and the tube pumps it straight into the hemocoel, the open cavity between the organs, instead of through any vessels.

compounds.name: Ganglion
compounds.fact: A cluster of neuron cell bodies acting as its own local nerve center — vertebrates reserve the word for structures outside the brain and spinal cord, but among invertebrates that restriction is dropped entirely, and the main mass of an insect's own brain is itself called the cerebral ganglion.

compounds.name: Ventral Nerve Cord
compounds.fact: Not a single cord along the back but a rope-ladder strung along the belly instead: physically separate ganglia at each segment, made of nervous tissue, linked lengthwise by connectives and rung by cross-tracts called commissures, carrying signal both up to the brain and back down to the body.

compounds.name: Ovariole
compounds.fact: The basic unit of egg production, not one shared ovary the way vertebrates have — a germarium of germline stem cells at the tip feeds a row of developing oocytes down the tube toward a shared duct, and the whole ovary is just a bundle of these tubes working in parallel.

compounds.name: Spermatheca
compounds.fact: A cuticle-lined tube or sac where sperm from mating is held in reserve, separate from fertilization itself — sperm sits here until an egg is ready to be fertilized on its way out, and by biasing which sperm gets used, the female keeps a say in whose offspring result long after mating is over.

compounds.name: Reptile Scale
compounds.fact: Keratinized epidermis thickened and folded into overlapping plates — the same protein family ordinary skin already uses, just packed denser. In turtles and crocodilians a plate of bone sits underneath as well; most snakes and lizards have no such backing.

compounds.name: Snake Skin
compounds.fact: Shed whole rather than flaked off piece by piece — the entire outer layer peels backward from head to tail in one go, the way a dust jacket comes off a book, leaving a fresh layer already grown underneath.

compounds.name: Snake Spine
compounds.fact: Between 175 and more than 400 vertebrae, almost every one of them carrying its own pair of movable ribs — and no living snake retains any trace of the shoulder girdle its four-legged ancestors had.

compounds.name: Snake Skull
compounds.fact: The lower jaw hinges to the skull through an extra bone, the quadrate, that most vertebrates don't have free this way — the added joint is what lets a snake work its mouth around prey wider than its own head.

compounds.name: Snake Lung
compounds.fact: One lung does almost all the work — the left lung is often small or missing outright, so in most species only the right lung is actually functional.

compounds.name: Vomeronasal Organ
compounds.fact: A second, separate sense of smell in the roof of the mouth: the forked tongue flicks out to collect particles from the air or ground, then touches them to this organ on the way back in for analysis.

compounds.name: Turtle Shell
compounds.fact: Fifty to sixty of the animal's own bones, not an add-on: the domed carapace is ribs and vertebrae fused outward, the flatter plastron is built from the shoulder girdle and sternum, and keratin scutes cap the whole thing.

compounds.name: Venom Gland
compounds.fact: A modified salivary gland, not a new invention — venom is made and stored in sac-like alveoli, wrapped in its own sheath of muscle, then travels down a duct to the base of the fangs.

compounds.name: Pit Organ
compounds.fact: A membrane strung between the eye and the nostril, so thick with heat-sensing nerve endings from the trigeminal nerve that infrared radiation alone forms a picture — evolved independently in pit vipers, boas and pythons.

compounds.name: Rattle
compounds.fact: Hollow keratin segments, made by modifying the ordinary scales at the tip of the tail and left interlocked after every shed instead of falling away — a dedicated 'shaker' muscle contracts to buzz them against each other.

compounds.name: Rumen
compounds.fact: The largest of a cow's four stomach compartments, and no cellulase of its own — millions of resident bacteria, archaea, protozoa and fungi ferment the cellulose instead, against a wall lined in fingerlike papillae built to absorb what they produce.

compounds.name: Abomasum
compounds.fact: The fourth and final stomach compartment, and the only one that works anything like ours — a true glandular stomach, secreting acid to break down the microbial and dietary protein the first three chambers already fermented.

compounds.name: Horn
compounds.fact: Where cattle carry them, horns are never shed — a core of live bone that starts as subcutaneous connective tissue and later fuses to the skull, sheathed for life in the same keratin protein as hoof and hair.

compounds.name: Udder
compounds.fact: Two pairs of mammary glands fused into one hanging mass, each alveolus lined in milk-secreting cells and wrapped in its own contractile myoepithelium — cattle nurse from four teats on the milk line near the groin, not the pair on a chest that primates and elephants use.

compounds.name: Blowhole
compounds.fact: A nostril, relocated — homologous with any other mammal's, moved by degrees to the top of the head. Toothed whales keep one; baleen whales split into two, set in a V. A muscular plug seals it on every dive and relaxes open again at the surface.

compounds.name: Blubber
compounds.fact: A vascularized layer of fat laced through with collagen fiber, up to 30 centimeters thick in the biggest whales and as much as half the animal's body mass — insulation that, unlike fur, doesn't compress and lose its effect under diving pressure.

compounds.name: Flipper
compounds.fact: A hand, paddled flat: shortened arm bones and elongated finger bones, the middle two fingers multiplying their own joints (hyperphalangy) instead of ending at a wrist. The shoulder is the only joint in the whole limb that still moves.

compounds.name: Whale Lung
compounds.fact: Every breath swaps up to 90% of total lung volume, against roughly 15% for a land mammal — but past about 100 meters down, water pressure compresses the lung nearly flat regardless, so the real oxygen reserve for a deep dive is stored in the muscle instead.

compounds.name: Gill
compounds.fact: Comb-like filaments folded into lamellae to maximize surface area, with water flowing over them in the direction opposite the blood inside — that countercurrent arrangement alone recovers as much as 90% of the oxygen dissolved in the water.

compounds.name: Fish Heart
compounds.fact: Two true chambers, not four — one atrium, one ventricle — pumping blood through a single loop: gills first, then straight on to the rest of the body, with no second pass back through the heart the way a bird's or mammal's blood gets.

compounds.name: Lateral Line
compounds.fact: A line of neuromasts under the skin, each one a cluster of hair cells capped by a flexible, jellylike cupula. Water movement bends the hairs, and that bend alone is what lets a fish sense vibration, pressure change and the pull of its own school.

compounds.name: Eggshell Membrane
compounds.fact: Two sheets of fibrous protein, mostly collagen type I, lining the shell's interior — outer and inner — that separate at the blunt end as the egg's contents cool and shrink after laying, opening the air cell between them.

compounds.name: Thick Albumen
compounds.fact: About 90% water carrying a dense tangle of dissolved protein — four times the ovomucin of the thin white around it, which is what gives it the gel-like body that cushions the yolk.

compounds.name: Thin Albumen
compounds.fact: The same 90% water and dissolved protein as the thick white beside it, just a quarter of the ovomucin — thin enough to run, which is why it spreads first the moment a shell cracks.

compounds.name: Chalazae
compounds.fact: Two spiral bands of albumen, twisted in opposite directions off each end of the yolk, doing one job: holding it suspended and centered in the white no matter which way the egg turns.

compounds.name: Vitelline Membrane
compounds.fact: Two layers of its own glycoproteins wrapping the yolk, structurally nothing like a cell membrane — it lets water and nutrients cross over from the white while still holding the yolk's shape.

compounds.name: Yolk Mass
compounds.fact: More than 90% of the yolk's own cytoplasm by the time of fertilization, packed into granules of lipid, protein and enzyme, with the fat alone outweighing the protein by nearly two to one.

compounds.name: Germinal Disc
compounds.fact: A small disc of cytoplasm only a couple of millimetres across, sitting on the yolk's surface at its animal pole — the one spot on the whole yolk built to become an embryo.

compounds.name: Yolk
compounds.fact: A membrane-wrapped sphere of stored fat and protein, suspended in the white by the chalazae and carrying one small disc of living cytoplasm on its surface.

compounds.name: Eggshell
compounds.fact: 95 to 97% calcium carbonate crystal, stabilized by its own protein matrix and grown in columns from proteoglycan-rich mammillae, capped with a thin outer cuticle and threaded with pores for gas exchange.

compounds.name: Air Cell
compounds.fact: A pocket of ordinary air trapped between the two shell membranes at the egg's blunt end, formed as the contents cool and shrink after laying — the bigger it grows in storage, the older the egg.

compounds.name: Sulfite Ion
compounds.fact: One sulfur, three oxygens and a lone pair, arranged pyramidal like ammonia — the ion at the core of every food-preservative sulfite salt.

compounds.name: Bisulfite Ion
compounds.fact: Sulfite with one proton added — the conjugate acid of sulfite and the conjugate base of sulfurous acid, sitting one rung apart from each on the same acid-base ladder.

compounds.name: Metabisulfite Ion
compounds.fact: Two bisulfite ions condense and shed a water molecule, welding an SO2 group onto an SO3 group through a single sulfur-sulfur bond — commonly called metabisulfite or pyrosulfite.

compounds.name: Sodium Sulfite
compounds.fact: E221. Sodium paired with the sulfite ion — an antioxidant and reducing agent that keeps dried fruit from browning and helps preserve meat.

compounds.name: Sodium Bisulfite
compounds.fact: E222. Not really a solid at all — the name for sodium and bisulfite ions dissolved together in water; try to crystallize it and what comes out is sodium metabisulfite instead. Bleaches starches and delays spoilage.

compounds.name: Sodium Metabisulfite
compounds.fact: E223. An antimicrobial and antioxidant behind a wine bottle's 'Contains Sulfites' label, and the chip shop's trick for keeping cut potatoes from browning before the fryer.

compounds.name: Potassium Metabisulfite
compounds.fact: E224. Sodium metabisulfite's potassium twin, chemically similar enough that the two are sometimes used interchangeably as a winemaking antioxidant and a source of disinfecting sulfur dioxide.

compounds.name: Calcium Sulfite
compounds.fact: E226. Calcium's version of the same oxygen-scavenging antioxidant, preserving wine, cider, fruit juice and canned produce; sodium and magnesium sulfites have mostly displaced it in industrial wood pulping.

compounds.name: Calcium Bisulfite
compounds.fact: E227. Calcium and two bisulfite ions, made by dosing lime with excess sulfur dioxide and water — used to brine cherries and, at industrial scale, to pulp wood into paper.

compounds.name: Potassium Bisulfite
compounds.fact: E228. Like its sodium counterpart, not a true solid but potassium and bisulfite ions in solution — used as a sterilising agent in brewing and winemaking.

compounds.name: Thyroid
compounds.fact: Follicles of epithelium wrapped around a protein-rich colloid core — the follicular cells draw in iodine to build thyroxine and triiodothyronine, while scattered C cells nearby make calcitonin instead, a second hormone system riding in the same gland.

compounds.name: Adrenal Gland
compounds.fact: Two glands stacked in one organ, not one: an outer cortex making steroid hormones — cortisol, aldosterone — and an inner medulla, developmentally more nerve tissue than gland, that fires adrenaline and noradrenaline straight into the bloodstream.

compounds.name: Pituitary Gland
compounds.fact: Two glands fused into one pea-sized organ at the base of the brain: a front lobe of secretory epithelium taking orders from the hypothalamus by blood, a rear lobe that is actually hypothalamus tissue itself, releasing hormones stored at the end of its own nerve fibers.

compounds.name: Pineal Gland
compounds.fact: A pea-sized cone of nervous tissue near the brain's center, evolved from cells related to the retina's own light sensors — it takes its timing cue from the eyes by way of the brain's clock, and answers only with melatonin, on darkness.

compounds.name: Thyroxine
compounds.fact: Four iodine atoms hung off a tyrosine backbone — the only hormone built around a halogen at all — secreted by the thyroid as a slow-acting store that peripheral tissue converts to the sharper triiodothyronine as needed.

compounds.name: Cortisol
compounds.fact: A steroid built in the adrenal cortex's zona fasciculata, released on a daily rhythm and again under stress — it raises blood sugar by favoring glucose over storage, and dials the immune system down while it's high.

compounds.name: Adrenaline
compounds.fact: Fired from the adrenal medulla in seconds, not the hours a steroid hormone takes — it is what actually arrives first in a fight-or-flight response, spiking heart rate and blood sugar before cortisol's slower rise catches up.

compounds.name: Melatonin
compounds.fact: Made from serotonin in the pineal gland, and only in the dark — light striking the retina suppresses it directly, which is the whole mechanism by which a bright screen at night keeps the brain from feeling sleepy.

compounds.name: Growth Hormone
compounds.fact: A single 191-amino-acid chain made by the anterior pituitary, not a steroid at all — it drives growth partly on its own and partly by pushing the liver to release IGF-1, the hormone that actually does most of the work on bone and muscle.

compounds.name: Lymph Node
compounds.fact: A fibrous capsule around a mesh of connective tissue, cortex packed with B cells in follicles and T cells in the paracortex beneath it — lymph slows to a crawl passing through, giving resident macrophages time to trap whatever it's carrying.

compounds.name: Spleen
compounds.fact: Red pulp and white pulp doing two different jobs in one capsule — red pulp macrophages filter worn-out red blood cells and recycle their iron, while white pulp holds the same B- and T-cell arrangement a lymph node does.

compounds.name: Thymus
compounds.fact: A scaffold of epithelial cells with immature T cells crowded through the mesh between them — cortex first, testing whether a T cell can recognize the body's own markers, before the medulla weeds out the ones that would attack the body itself.

compounds.name: Lymph
compounds.fact: Interstitial fluid once it's been collected into a vessel — closer to blood plasma than anything else, richer in lymphocytes by the time it leaves a node, and the only route fat absorbed in the gut has to reach the bloodstream at all.

compounds.name: Eosinophil
compounds.fact: One to three percent of white blood cells, named for how eagerly its granules soak up the red dye eosin — its actual job is multicellular parasites, too big for a single phagocyte to swallow whole.

compounds.name: Basophil
compounds.fact: The rarest white blood cell in circulation, under one percent — it carries histamine and heparin in its granules and fires them on an allergen, which is most of what an allergic reaction actually is.

compounds.name: Macrophage
compounds.fact: What a monocyte becomes within a day or three of leaving the bloodstream for tissue — it engulfs pathogens and debris whole through phagocytosis, then breaks them down in a fused phagosome-lysosome before signaling other immune cells in.

compounds.name: Eye
compounds.fact: Light crosses the cornea for most of its bending, passes through an iris-ringed pupil that sets how much gets in, gets fine-focused by the lens, and lands on the retina, which is the only part that actually senses it.

compounds.name: Cornea
compounds.fact: Five layers doing most of the eye's focusing before light ever reaches the lens — kept perfectly transparent by having no blood vessels at all, drawing its oxygen straight from tear film instead.

compounds.name: Lens
compounds.fact: A biconvex capsule of crystallin protein packed in concentric fiber layers like an onion, kept clear by fiber cells that discard their own nucleus and mitochondria — with no blood vessels reaching in, it feeds entirely off the fluid bathing it.

compounds.name: Retina
compounds.fact: Ten stacked layers of nervous tissue at the back of the eye, photoreceptors facing away from the light so it has to pass through the whole stack first — about 92 million rods for dim light far outnumber the roughly 6 million cones that handle color and detail.

compounds.name: Iris
compounds.fact: Two smooth-muscle rings working against each other — one circular to shrink the pupil, one radial to widen it — fronted by a pigmented layer whose melanin decides eye color and blocks any light that isn't going through the pupil.

compounds.name: Rod Cell
compounds.fact: Sensitive enough to fire on a single photon, about a hundred times more so than a cone — the roughly 92 million of them in a human retina are what night vision runs on, at the cost of color and fine detail.

compounds.name: Cone Cell
compounds.fact: Three types, each carrying a different opsin protein tuned to red, green or blue wavelengths — comparing how strongly each type fires against the others is the entire mechanism behind seeing color at all.

compounds.name: Ear
compounds.fact: Three sections in series, not one organ: an outer funnel to the eardrum, a middle chamber of three tiny bones to amplify its vibration, and a fluid-filled inner spiral that turns that vibration into the signal the brain hears.

compounds.name: Eardrum
compounds.fact: Three layers — skin outside, mucosa inside, a fibrous layer of collagen fibers holding the shape between them — stretched taut enough to bridge the middle ear's air and the inner ear's fluid, converting one kind of vibration into the other.

compounds.name: Ossicles
compounds.fact: Malleus, incus and stapes — the three smallest bones in the body, the stapes smallest of all — forming a lever chain across the middle ear that turns the eardrum's vibration into enough force to move fluid on the other side.

compounds.name: Cochlea
compounds.fact: A fluid-filled spiral making almost three full turns, its basilar membrane stiff near the base and floppy near the tip so different points along its length answer to different pitches — hair cells riding that membrane are what actually turn the vibration into nerve signal.

compounds.name: Hair Cell
compounds.fact: Named for the tuft of stereocilia on top that bends with the slightest vibration, opening ion channels that fire a nerve signal — the human inner ear cannot regrow a damaged one, which is why hearing loss from noise or age is permanent.

compounds.name: Epidermis
compounds.fact: Four or five layers of keratinocytes, nine tenths of the cells here, replaced completely about every 48 days — and with no blood supply of its own, fed only by oxygen diffusing straight from the air.

compounds.name: Dermis
compounds.fact: Dense connective tissue in two layers, papillary and reticular, laced with collagen and elastic fibers — its blood vessels feed the bloodless epidermis above, and its nerve endings are what let skin feel anything at all.

compounds.name: Hypodermis
compounds.fact: Loose connective tissue packed with fat cells beneath the dermis — padding, an energy reserve, a layer of insulation, and the fibrous bands that anchor skin down to whatever lies underneath it.

compounds.name: Melanocyte
compounds.fact: Sits in the epidermis's deepest layer and packages melanin into organelles called melanosomes, handing them off to nearby keratinocytes — the pigment is dark enough to absorb most UV light before it gets any deeper.

compounds.name: Hair Follicle
compounds.fact: An organ in its own right, built around a connective-tissue papilla and its capillary loop, with a matrix of dividing cells producing new hair — a tiny arrector pili muscle attaches to it and pulls it upright, which is the entire mechanism behind a goosebump.

compounds.name: Sweat Gland
compounds.fact: Two kinds doing different jobs: eccrine glands nearly everywhere on the body cool it by evaporating a watery sweat, while apocrine glands confined to the armpits and groin secrete a thicker fluid that bacteria turn into odor.

compounds.name: Sebaceous Gland
compounds.fact: Attached to nearly every hair follicle, it makes sebum by holocrine secretion — the gland's own cells rupture and die to release it, an oily coating that lubricates skin and hair and helps waterproof both.

compounds.name: Nail
compounds.fact: Hardened alpha-keratin, the same protein family as claws, hooves and horns, pushed forward continuously by a matrix of dividing cells at its root — fingernails grow about 3.5 millimeters a month, toenails roughly half that.

compounds.name: Nephron
compounds.fact: The kidney's working unit, one to one and a half million per kidney — a filtering corpuscle feeding a long tubule, running filtration, reabsorption, secretion and excretion in sequence to turn blood plasma into urine.

compounds.name: Glomerulus
compounds.fact: A tuft of capillaries packed inside Bowman's capsule at the start of every nephron — podocytes wrap each vessel and, together with the capillary wall itself, filter blood plasma into the fluid that becomes urine.

compounds.name: Renal Tubule
compounds.fact: A long pipe of cuboidal epithelium running from Bowman's capsule through the loop of Henle to a collecting duct — its first stretch alone reclaims 80% of filtered glucose and over half the filtered salt and water.

compounds.name: Ureter
compounds.fact: A 20-to-30-centimeter tube of stretch-tolerant urothelium wrapped in two, then three, layers of smooth muscle in its lower third — nothing drains through it by gravity, it is pushed toward the bladder by peristalsis alone.

compounds.name: Bladder
compounds.fact: A hollow organ lined with transitional urothelium three to six cell layers deep, holding 300 to 500 milliliters before the urge to empty it starts — the detrusor, a smooth-muscle coat spiraling through the wall, is what does the emptying.

compounds.name: Urethra
compounds.fact: About 4 centimeters long in a woman, 18 to 20 in a man, whose urethra also carries semen — the lining shifts from transitional cells near the bladder to flatter cells near the outer opening.

compounds.name: Urea
compounds.fact: Assembled in the liver's urea cycle from the ammonia that amino-acid breakdown leaves behind — it makes up more than half the dissolved solids in urine, the body's main way of shedding nitrogen it can't use.

compounds.name: Urine
compounds.fact: About 91 to 96% water carrying dissolved urea, salts and other metabolic leftovers — roughly a liter and a half of it a day is how the kidneys clear the bloodstream of what it doesn't need.

compounds.name: Testis
compounds.fact: Coiled seminiferous tubules doing the sperm-making, with Leydig cells packed in the connective tissue between tubules doing something entirely different — making the testosterone that puberty runs on.

compounds.name: Seminiferous Tubule
compounds.fact: Its lining is Sertoli cells, tall columnar cells nursing developing sperm cells through meiosis between them — this coiled tube inside the testis is the one place in the body spermatozoa are actually made.

compounds.name: Epididymis
compounds.fact: Six meters of duct coiled onto the back of each testis, its pseudostratified lining backed by smooth muscle that thickens from head to tail — sperm arrive unable to swim or fertilize anything and spend two to six days here gaining both.

compounds.name: Vas Deferens
compounds.fact: No other hollow organ has a higher muscle-to-lumen ratio — three thick layers of smooth muscle wrapped around a narrow pseudostratified core, built to contract hard on ejaculation and drive sperm forward by peristalsis alone.

compounds.name: Seminal Vesicle
compounds.fact: A pair of convoluted glands behind the bladder supplying 70 to 85% of semen's volume — fructose and citric acid from its own secretion are what give sperm the fuel to keep swimming after ejaculation.

compounds.name: Prostate
compounds.fact: Glandular tissue wrapped in fibrous and smooth-muscle connective tissue, doubling as the mechanical switch between urination and ejaculation — its own secretion makes up close to 30% of semen's volume.

compounds.name: Penis
compounds.fact: Two parallel corpora cavernosa and a single corpus spongiosum carrying the urethra through it — all three are blood sinusoids meshed through sheets of connective tissue, and filling those sinusoids with blood is the entire mechanism of an erection.

compounds.name: Ovary
compounds.fact: About a million follicles are present at birth and only around one in two thousand will ever ovulate — between cycles of releasing an egg, the gland also secretes estrogen and progesterone straight into the bloodstream.

compounds.name: Ovarian Follicle
compounds.fact: A single oocyte ringed by granulosa cells and, past a basement membrane, two further layers called the theca — roughly once a month, one follicle in the whole ovary wins the competition to release its egg.

compounds.name: Fallopian Tube
compounds.fact: Cilia on its columnar lining beat in time with muscular contractions to carry an egg from ovary to uterus — the ampulla, its widest stretch, is where a released egg is actually fertilized, not the uterus itself.

compounds.name: Uterus
compounds.fact: Three layers, inside out: endometrium, where a blastocyst implants and which is shed monthly if none does; myometrium, smooth muscle thick enough to deliver a baby; and perimetrium, a thin connective-tissue coat over the outside.

compounds.name: Cervix
compounds.fact: Smooth muscle and fibrous connective tissue around a canal lined in two kinds of epithelium — mucus output multiplies tenfold around ovulation, and the same tissue that stays rigid all cycle must dilate past 10 centimeters in labor.

compounds.name: Vagina
compounds.fact: A fibromuscular canal: stratified squamous epithelium inside, circular and longitudinal smooth muscle around that, and an outer connective-tissue adventitia — built to serve as birth canal, menstrual outlet and copulatory passage all at once.

compounds.name: Placenta
compounds.fact: Grows from the trophoblast, the blastocyst's own outer layer, into an organ shared by two separate circulatory systems — maternal and fetal blood exchange gases and nutrients across a barrier without ever actually mixing.

compounds.name: Mammary Gland
compounds.fact: A modified sweat gland: alveoli of milk-secreting cells wrapped in contractile myoepithelial cells, grouped into lobules — a suckling infant triggers oxytocin, and oxytocin is what actually squeezes the milk out.

compounds.name: Testosterone
compounds.fact: Made by Leydig cells inside the testis, this steroid drives the development of the testes and prostate themselves and then keeps building on top of that — more muscle and bone mass, more body hair, most of what puberty does to a male body.

compounds.name: Estradiol
compounds.fact: The predominant estrogen through a woman's reproductive years, produced in ovarian follicles among other tissues — it builds breast tissue and hip width at puberty, then keeps running the menstrual cycle every month after.

compounds.name: Progesterone
compounds.fact: Poured out by the corpus luteum after ovulation, this steroid converts the endometrium into its secretory phase — the uterine lining a fertilized egg actually needs in order to implant at all.

$comment_atoms: The full periodic table is present as a reference set. Only those marked inPlay carry authored text and appear in a provenance tree today; the rest are here so later domains (metallurgy, medicine) have somewhere to attach, and so the table reads as complete to a curious player.
$comment_visual: kind drives shape (atom=periodic tile, compound=hexagon, particle=glow) and category drives colour. Categories are assigned by atomic number and checked for gaps and overlaps at build time.

aminos.name: Glycine
aminos.fact: The smallest, and the only one with no handedness.

aminos.name: Alanine
aminos.fact: The simplest with a side chain: a single carbon.

aminos.name: Serine
aminos.fact: Its spare hydroxyl is where cells attach switches.

aminos.name: Cysteine
aminos.fact: Two of these bond to each other and staple a protein shut.

aminos.name: Threonine
aminos.fact: Essential — you must eat it, you cannot build it.

aminos.name: Valine
aminos.fact: A single swap for glutamate here causes sickle-cell anaemia.

aminos.name: Leucine
aminos.fact: The commonest amino acid in most proteins.

aminos.name: Isoleucine
aminos.fact: Same formula as leucine, different shape entirely.

aminos.name: Proline
aminos.fact: Its ring kinks the chain — it is the corner piece.

aminos.name: Phenylalanine
aminos.fact: The one people with PKU cannot process.

aminos.name: Tyrosine
aminos.fact: Raw material for adrenaline, dopamine and melanin.

aminos.name: Tryptophan
aminos.fact: The largest, and the precursor of serotonin.

aminos.name: Aspartate
aminos.fact: Half of aspartame.

aminos.name: Glutamate
aminos.fact: Tastes savoury on its own — this is umami.

aminos.name: Asparagine
aminos.fact: First isolated from asparagus, in 1806.

aminos.name: Glutamine
aminos.fact: The most abundant free amino acid in your blood.

aminos.name: Lysine
aminos.fact: Scarce in cereals, which is why beans and grain go together.

aminos.name: Arginine
aminos.fact: Four nitrogens: the most nitrogen-rich of the twenty.

aminos.name: Histidine
aminos.fact: Sits in enzyme active sites, passing protons about.

aminos.name: Methionine
aminos.fact: Every protein starts here — it is what START codes for.

tiers.name: Particles
tiers.blurb: Not matter. Energy, and the things smaller than atoms.

tiers.name: Elements
tiers.blurb: The periodic table. Ninety-odd of these make everything.

tiers.name: Molecules
tiers.blurb: Atoms bonded into a fixed recipe. Water, salt, quartz.

tiers.name: Monomers
tiers.blurb: Single links, built to be chained: sugars, amino acids, nucleotides.

tiers.name: Polymers
tiers.blurb: Monomers joined into chains. Almost all of life is chains.

tiers.name: Structures
tiers.blurb: A chain folded into a shape. In biology, shape is function.

tiers.name: Assemblies
tiers.blurb: Structures working together: membranes, machines, organelles.

tiers.name: Cells
tiers.blurb: The smallest thing that is unambiguously alive.

tiers.name: Blood Cells
tiers.blurb: The formed elements suspended in blood plasma — most are living cells doing one specific job, but a mature red cell has no nucleus left and a platelet was never a whole cell to begin with.

tiers.name: Tissues
tiers.blurb: Cells of one kind, doing one job together.

tiers.name: Tubes
tiers.blurb: Chitin-lined channels that carry air from an opening in the body wall straight to the cells that need it — no lungs, no vessels, no blood involved.

tiers.name: Bones
tiers.blurb: Collagen and mineral cast into a shape, built for load, leverage or protection.

tiers.name: Fluids
tiers.blurb: Water carrying dissolved protein, doing one job without ever setting solid.

tiers.name: Organs
tiers.blurb: Different tissues, working together as one structure with one job.

tiers.name: Joints
tiers.blurb: Where two bones meet — cushioned, lubricated, and held together well enough to move without touching.

tiers.name: Egg Structures
tiers.blurb: Built around a single cell before it ever leaves the body — shell, membrane, white and yolk, secreted rather than grown from living tissue.

linkages.name: Peptide bond
linkages.fact: A carboxyl meets an amine, and one water molecule leaves. That is why a residue in a chain weighs less than the free acid.

linkages.name: Glycosidic bond
linkages.fact: Sugar to sugar, also losing water. Whether it points up or down decides starch from cellulose.

linkages.name: Phosphodiester bond
linkages.fact: Phosphate bridging two sugars. This is the backbone DNA hangs its letters on.

linkages.name: Ester bond
linkages.fact: Fatty acid to glycerol. Three of them make a fat.

linkages.name: Hydrogen bonding
linkages.fact: Individually feeble, collectively decisive. It holds the helix, the sheet, and water itself together.

linkages.name: Folding
linkages.fact: The chain collapses into one specific shape, usually in under a second. Get it wrong and you have a prion.
